cells.tense: The pen is in your hand now, and what moves in you and what you do are one line.
cells.ask: Think of one person you're close to. Get into the same room and sit near them — shoulder's width, not across the table — and say one plain sentence about what matters to you right now. Then stay twenty minutes.
cells.core:
You can feel with someone and keep your own center at the same time. That's what lets you stay turned toward people instead of managing them. What you feel and the direction you're going stay in one line, so care shows up in what you actually do about it, and it doesn't cost you your footing. That steadiness gets felt by them, even when neither of you names it.

What you're free to feed next is the ease of making something with someone. When you stay close and stay aligned with yourself, a shared plan or a shared piece of work becomes possible. That's replenishing, not effortful, because the feeling is what carries it. You can put one such thing in motion this week — a call, a decision made together, a small yes — and let the energy come from the connection itself, not from pushing.
cells.sheetLine: Care shows up in what you do, and people can lean on that.
cells.verb: moving in the same direction as what you feel
cells.place: the room where you feel both for and with, and stay reachable

cells.tense: You're already bracing for a future conversation that hasn't happened, writing both sides of it before the other person opens their mouth.
cells.ask: When the feeling surges tonight, write three lines no one will see: what you're bracing for, one thing that's actually true now, and one small thing you could do tomorrow. Then put the page in a drawer and don't act on it until morning.
cells.core:
You overload the connection, trying to make people feel what you feel ahead of time. You anticipate their side, their reaction, the exact shape of the room, and you do it in advance — which is a kind of care, but it arrives as pressure. You think you're preparing; you're actually writing a future that hasn't happened, and the people in front of you get the rehearsal instead of you. Feeling doesn't need to be defended. It needs a place to land.

When the surge comes, sit down with it before you bring it to anyone. Three lines: what you're braced for, what's true right now, and one small next step. When the noise settles enough to hear yourself, you can choose what to say and when. The person gets something real to answer instead of a guess you already made.
cells.sheetLine: You're writing tomorrow's conversation before today's has a chance.
cells.verb: moving in the same direction as what you feel
cells.place: the room where you feel both for and with, and stay reachable

cells.tense: The pen is down and you're watching from the far side of the room you used to stand in.
cells.ask: Text one person and name one real thing from your week. Not a full account — one sentence that's true. Send it and let whatever answer comes be the whole exercise.
cells.core:
You stopped reaching, and it got quiet. Being with people is a place you watch from a little distance now, and you're careful there, calling it being considerate. The feeling didn't go anywhere. The moving-toward someone stopped.

Start with the dry ground you're standing on and let it grow something small. Tell one person one true thing from your week — not the whole story, just one plain piece — and stop there. That's enough to let a connection begin again without demanding you open the whole door at once. When it's answered, that reply is the whole result. You don't have to grow it or fix it or follow it up.

cells.tense: You're holding what someone near you feels, and you'd call that just being practical.
cells.ask: Pick one concern you're holding for someone else and say to their face, "I've been carrying this for you — it's yours." Then spend an hour on something that's only yours, with nothing on the way back.
cells.core:
You feel with people easily. You read the room, you catch the small shift in someone's voice, you adjust before anyone asks. You'd call that being practical — but the connection is running, and your own direction has slipped out of the frame. The feeling is doing real work on their behalf; it's the saying-so that's missing, and somewhere in the mix your own moving-forward has gone quiet.

The one who isn't named in this is you. Hand one of those carried things back — say it plainly, once — then spend an hour on something that's only yours, not scheduled around anyone else. That keeps the feeling and puts your direction back in the same line with it, so being with people happens on purpose instead of by drift.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding someone's feeling and calling your own direction logistics.
cells.verb: moving in the same direction as what you feel
cells.place: the room where you feel both for and with, and stay reachable
